item.title: Georgia ICE sweep nabs over 700 criminal illegal aliens including sex offenders, child abusers
item.description: Operation Safe Community in Atlanta, Georgia netted over 1,200 immigration arrests, with DHS saying 720 had criminal histories including sex crimes.
item.content:encoded:
Federal immigration officers arrested more than 1,200 illegal immigrants in the Atlanta, Georgia area, including 720 who DHS said had been convicted of or charged with crimes.

Speaking on "Fox & Friends," Marcos Charles, executive associate director of ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, said the sweep took violent criminals — including sex offenders and child abusers — off the streets.

"We arrested over 1,200 aliens, illegal aliens, out in the Atlanta, Georgia area. More than half of those people had criminal histories," Charles said.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

"We're talking about sex crimes, assault and battery, some with DUI convictions, domestic violence. These individuals needed to be taken off the street, not only because they're criminals, but because they are here illegally in the United States," he added.

The Department of Homeland Security announced online that the sweep, called "Operation Safe Community – Atlanta," focused on criminal illegal immigrants. 

"Every day, the men and women of ICE ERO were out in the streets across the nation, enforcing the immigration laws as set forth by Congress. So we're keeping the community safe. We're [going to] be traveling all over the United States doing the same thing," Charles said.

In July, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded approximately 51,000 immigration arrests, which ICE said was its highest monthly total ever, surpassing the 43,000 arrests recorded in June.

TRUMP DHS CHIEF UNDER FIRE FROM CONSERVATIVES AFTER IMMIGRATION SPEECH IGNITES BACKLASH

Charles said agents have adapted their tactics because of protests and what he described as efforts to interfere with arrests, including changes to how they track individuals in the country illegally.

"What we've done is we've adapted to that, not only with additional training, but we've adapted our methodology on how we conduct these enforcement efforts and our arrest methods," he said.

Among those arrested, DHS identified a Mexican national with prior convictions for "conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine and driving while intoxicated."

DHS also identified an illegal immigrant from El Salvador with prior arrests for "domestic battery/family violence, cruelty to children, disorderly conduct and driving while intoxicated."

ICE SAYS OFFICER SHOT AND KILLED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO TRIED TO RAM HIM WITH CAR IN HOUSTON

The operation comes months after DHS reported an 8,000% increase in death threats against ICE officers. Some progressive lawmakers have also called for abolishing ICE over concerns about the agency's enforcement operations.

item.title: Protect College Sports Act stalls in overnight Senate showdown, vote pushed to September after chaotic evening
item.description: The Protect College Sports Act stalled Friday as senators filed amendments targeting conference realignment, women's sports, and NCAA liability.
item.content:encoded:
What looked like a last-minute lifeline for the 'Protect College Sports Act' turned into a 2 a.m. Senate dead end, even in spite of a late push from President Donald Trump.

After a frantic Friday filled with amendments, objections and pressure from the President to keep lawmakers in Washington, supporters believed they had a path to a vote before the August recess.

Senators and aides were called back to the Capitol late Friday night as momentum appeared to be building.

But in the early morning hours on Saturday, that push came up short. Unfortunately for Senators Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., along with Eric Schmitt, R-Mo, they could not garner enough support for a vote.

TED CRUZ URGES SENATE TO STAY IN WASHINGTON UNTIL PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT PASSES THIS WEEK

"The Protect College Sports Act continues to show great momentum. Sens Cruz and Schmitt have worked tirelessly with the support of nearly every conference in the country, HBCUs and the Olympic sports committee. It's clear that this bill is the only way to save college sports and women’s sports," Cruz and Schmitt said in a statement early Saturday morning.

"While we are disappointed that we could not get the unanimous consent agreement to finish this week, we locked in a guaranteed vote in September. With the strong support of President Trump, we look forward to him signing the bill on college game day in the Fall."

In what turned out to be an intense day of negotiations, Senators from both sides of the aisle met numerous times to discuss the legislation that kept college athletic officials and reporters glued to their phones over the previous 72 hours.

When the SEC and Big Ten voted to put their support behind the bipartisan legislation just one week ago, there was hope among everyone involved that they could get the bill to the Senate floor and send it to the House before the congressional recess.

On Friday, with the deadline creeping up on those looking to push this legislation through, a bevy of amendments were filed by Senators looking to enhance the bill in their eyes.

After days of anticipation about whether this 'NIL Bill' would actually be taken up for a vote, Senate aides were scrambling early Saturday morning to make their way back to the Capitol.

But, the intense negotiations turned into all sides laying down their swords, until September.

"Time may have run out to protect college sports in August, but there is plenty of time in September," Senator Maria Cantwell said in a statement. "I'm glad Senator Thune set a date certain in September to bring it up because the challenges facing student athletes and universities aren't going away.

"The Protect College Sports Act provides stability and gives first-ever federal NIL rights and scholarship and healthcare protections for athletes. And this bipartisan bill is how we protect women's and Olympic sports. I look forward to its passage in September."

Even with a push from President Donald Trump, this legislation was fighting against time, objections and the Senate 'hotline' that is used to essentially determine whether a bill would actually have the support to be voted on.

It was actually Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) who filed the most intriguing amendment to the PCSA, taking issue with the five-year independent section that would force schools to abandon their conferences, like the ACC, for a number of years before being allowed to join another.

This has been an issue discussed by many across the ACC and Big 12 in previous weeks, wondering aloud what this would prevent in terms of being raided by the others, most notably the SEC.

Right now, under its current form, conferences would only be allowed to have 19 member schools in their league.

But, in terms of a school having to become independent for five years before joining a different conference, the issue was brought up by Senator Moody that it could benefit schools like Florida State or Miami in her home state, along with a number of others that have taken issue with the ACC in previous years.

The amendment would provide a 180-day window for schools to opt-out of their current conference before the law would go into effect, if it actually ever does. But, this realignment provision provides schools the opportunity to avoid the 5-year independent clause and start the process of moving on without punishment.

If you think the ongoing issues between the NCAA and student-athletes suing for a fifth year of eligibility are wild, just wait until a number of schools try to jump ship and join a new conference before Christmas arrives.

Don't forget, Florida State and Clemson sued the ACC in 2023 over language in the conference's 'Grant of Rights' pertaining to how much it would cost for schools to leave before the ACC's television contract was set to expire.

While this might seem like a Senator doing her home-state school a solid, this 'independent' provision had already received pushback from plenty of leaders behind the scenes.

Whether those within Senate offices pushing for a bill to pass this week wanted to admit it, getting this to the floor for a vote was always a tall task, especially with time not on their side.

As of late afternoon Friday, there were 10 different holds and objections to the bill being expedited for a vote, with an additional eight holds pertaining to the PCSA on its own. Early Saturday morning, while there were still 'holds' (objections) to the bill, that number had been reduced considerably.

Without unanimous support, along with the 60 votes of support needed to pass the bill, an actual vote was still being worked on from those involved.

REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS

Senator John Kennedy (R-LA) took a shot at the legislation on Friday, aiming his comments towards providing the NCAA with enhanced protection that some do not want to provide on a broad basis.

"Make sure that this legislation doesn’t — either intentionally or unintentionally — absolve the NCAA, which lacks testicles and a spine, of any liability," Burgess Everrett reported.

Also, there was pushback from outside the nation's Capitol centered around the protection of women's sports under this legislation, with Riley Gaines writing that this bill in its current form has a 'fatal flaw', arguing that this would give transgender athletes legal grounds to challenge state eligibility rules.

Friday afternoon, White House counsel released a letter to congressional leaders emphasizing that the 'Protect College Sports Act' would not preempt current state laws that prohibit men for competing in women's sports.

"States may still legislate on the question of whether trans individuals should play on men's team or women's team."

And then, when you throw in the National Black Caucus releasing its own statement on not being able to support the bill in its current form, the likelihood of the PCSA actually garnering enough support started to feel as though it was slipping away in a more significant way.

This dragging into the college football season was always going to happen, no matter if the Senate took a vote this weekend or not.

The amendment process is going to take a lot more time than Friday provided, even if Senators decided to stick around for an additional day.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Then, if it passed through the Senate, there were going to be potential changes made in the House before a vote would take place on this part of the congressional ladder.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Right now, this is going to lead into September and beyond, with midterms upcoming and other key issues for leaders.

So, here we are, with those in favor of the 'Protect College Sports Act' trying to keep its hopes of becoming law alive amidst pushback and proposed amendments.

It's going to be a long few months ahead.

item.title: Dem Senate hopeful flip-flops on emerging issue impacting communities across US
item.description: Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown celebrated Amazon datacenter construction in Ohio in 2015 but now campaigns against them as an electric grid drain.
item.content:encoded:
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown once praised data center expansion, records show, even as he now runs on a platform opposing their development in a bid to return to the Senate.

In 2015, Brown put out a press release celebrating the construction of a third data center in Central Ohio.

"This new data center is great news for New Albany and central Ohio. Amazon’s growth in central Ohio signals that this region is not only a great place to do business, but a place where people want to live and raise a family," Brown said.

Now, just over 10 years later, Brown is painting Ohio’s 226 data centers as a drain on the state’s resources — a reversal that demonstrates how many Democrats have aligned themselves on the issue to press the case for affordability.

WATCH: GOP SENATOR UNLOADS ON 'CREATURE OF WASHINGTON' CHALLENGER IN CRITICAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

"Ohio’s electric grid — big corporations treat it like a game," Brown said in a recent campaign video.

"[They’re] gobbling up energy to feed their data centers no matter how much it raises our prices. It’s the latest way they’ve rigged the system."

Brown, who was originally elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006, lost re-election in 2024 to Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio. Now he is waging a comeback bid for Ohio’s other Senate seat against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted.

Husted, who has not yet won a full term in the Senate, was appointed by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine to fill the seat of now-former Sen. J.D. Vance, R-Ohio, when Trump tapped him to become vice president.

In the 2026 midterms, Democrats have hammered President Donald Trump and what they see as unfulfilled promises to bring down the cost of everyday items like food, fuel and housing.

While slightly removed from those specific items, an increasing number of Democrats, like Brown, have tied data centers to the issue, arguing that they do little to pay for their own costs in terms of water and electrical use. In their view, data centers are being subsidized by the communities where they’re being built.

FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC UNITY, REPUBLICAN CROSSOVERS SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE

Debates remain about whether their consumption has meaningfully changed utility rates in local communities and, if so, whether the companies should pay for the costs of their consumption.

Brown said he would support legislation along those lines.

"I’ll require the data centers to pay the full cost of their own electricity — not you," Brown said.

Ohio, in particular, has become an increasingly important state in the data center conversation as companies like Amazon and Google have sought out state incentives for their construction.

In 2013, the state legislature passed tax exemptions for the "sale, storage, use or other consumption of computer data center equipment." The law gives the Ohio Tax Credit Authority (TCA) the power to approve tax exemptions for companies that invest more than $100 million over three consecutive years. Not all centers are automatically qualified to participate in the benefit and can receive a partial exemption.

The move has attracted sizeable investment but also cost the state $1.6 billion in forgone revenue in 2025, according to the Ohio 2026-2027 Tax Expenditure Report.

It’s unclear if Brown would support more than just a requirement that data centers pay for their electricity and whether he would consider other legislation to slow their development. In his 2015 press release, Brown noted that the centers had created new job opportunities with their openings.

TOP ENERGY GROUP WARNS WEALTHY FOREIGNERS ARE POTENTIALLY BANKROLLING ANTI-DATA CENTER CAMPAIGNS ACROSS US

"I look forward to working to ensure that our region’s burgeoning logistics hub continues to grow – creating good jobs for Ohioans and helping businesses prosper," Brown wrote.

His office did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital about the scope of his objections to data center developments in Ohio.

Having secured his party’s nomination for the seat, Brown will face Husted in the state’s Nov. 3 general election.

item.title: Socialism’s campus appeal meets Gen Z resistance as students keep score on communism
item.description: John Fetterman joined 800 pro-Israel students in Washington as socialist primary wins signal a leftward shift reshaping Democrats' stance on Israel.
item.content:encoded:
Pro-Israel college students who have watched socialism and anti-Israel activism gain ground on campus say the same political currents are now colliding with the Democratic Party — and the backlash is pushing some young Jewish voters to the right.

"Even before the craziness of the post-October 7 campus climate, it was already an underlying sense of, 'America is bad and we're gonna learn about that,'" University of Michigan rising senior Addison Stone told Fox News Digital.

Speaking at the Israel on Campus Coalition’s national summit in Washington this week, students said political currents they have watched spread on college campuses are increasingly surfacing in Democratic politics, particularly as the party’s progressive wing gains ground and clashes deepen over Israel.

Dylan Goldman, a rising senior at UC Berkeley, identified himself as "left leaning" and told Fox News Digital that Democratic lawmakers welcoming the popular socialist candidates – who overwhelmingly hold hostile postures toward Israel – are making a "really poor move."

DEMOCRATS LURE ‘POLITICALLY HOMELESS’ GEN Z TOWARD SOCIALISM — A COUNTERATTACK IS TAKING SHAPE

"Jewish Democrats who are not single-issue voters... now feel so alienated by our own party that it’s pushing us conservative. It’s pushing to go further right," said Goldman.

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive whose campaign drew support from the democratic socialist movement, won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary Tuesday, adding to a string of victories for left-wing candidates challenging the Democratic establishment as the party battles for control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.

The conference brought hundreds of pro-Israel students to Washington for advocacy training, networking and discussions on supporting Israel, combating antisemitism and strengthening the U.S.-Israel relationship on college campuses.

"The academics don't help, but they're sort of helping indoctrinate the next generation and the next generation with the combination of learning about that in classes and going on social media and seeing it and the DSA trying to make everything cool with communism," Stone said. "You're really seeing the outcome of that on college campuses where they're burning both American and Israeli flags."

JEWISH MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS ADMIT THEY WILL VOTE REPUBLICAN IF ABDUL EL-SAYED BECOMES NOMINEE

As those political divisions play out nationally, organizers at the summit said Jewish students are still confronting the campus hostility that helped bring many of them to Washington.

"What’s happening to Jewish students on American campuses should alarm every American," Israel on Campus Coalition CEO Jacob Baime told Fox News Digital. "The hostility is out in the open now: mobs on the quad, intimidation in the classroom, and harassment online. But here’s what the mob didn’t count on: this generation isn’t backing down."

"These students are the proudest, toughest, most organized pro-Israel cohort we have ever seen. This week we brought more than 1000 campus leaders to Washington to train and equip them with the skills they need to go back to campus ready to fight for what they believe in," he added.

FETTERMAN WINS PRAISE FOR 'GUTS' AFTER GOING TOE-TO-TOE WITH JON STEWART OVER ISRAEL SUPPORT

Fetterman, who spoke at the Israel on Campus Coalition’s flagship event, said the Democratic Party’s shifting posture toward Israel and the Jewish community is becoming increasingly consequential.

His support for Israel has repeatedly put him at odds with members of his own party, including over the broader conflict in the Middle East and his backing of President Donald Trump’s strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.

"I think I was the only Democrat to support the Trump administration to bomb the Iranian nuclear facilities," Fetterman told Fox News Digital. "If you don’t want them to acquire a nuclear bomb, it’s pretty reasonable to bomb their nuclear facilities."

Fetterman argued the threat extends beyond Israel, casting the confrontation with Iran as a larger battle over American values and the West’s role in the region.

"The problem is Iran. That’s the problem," he said, later adding, "I’m proud to stand for America, civilization, democracy, and Israel is our special ally that represents all of that in that region."

item.title: America's cult-favorite grocery store cake has fans declaring it's 'worth the hype'
item.description: The Berry Chantilly Cake from Whole Foods Market originated 13 years ago at a New Orleans store and became a cult favorite served at weddings and birthday parties.
item.content:encoded:
A cake sold by Whole Foods Market is so beloved by customers, it's served at birthdays and weddings — and some people attest to eating it weekly.

The market's Berry Chantilly Cake "features layers of delicate vanilla cake, fluffy Chantilly cream frosting and fresh berries," the Whole Foods website says. "It's so irresistible, in fact, that people have been known to stand in line for it through power outages and impending natural disasters (true story)."

The cake has taken on various iterations over the years, including parfaits and a Berry Chantilly Latte as coffee bars experienced their own viral moment in 2025.

LINES WRAP AROUND BLOCK AS CUSTOMERS WAIT HOURS FOR VIRAL DOT CAKES THAT SELL OUT WITHIN MINUTES

Whole Foods refers to the cake as a "cult favorite," and social media posts support that claim.

A Reddit thread posted a few years ago asking whether the Berry Chantilly Cake was worth trying drew overwhelmingly enthusiastic, nearly unanimous praise.

"We had this as our wedding cutting cake!" responded one person. "I enjoyed it and wished I could have had more (but was full, was busy, etc.)."

"It's magic," replied another. "And there's a full cake size and half cake and 1/4 cake size, then a giant cupcake and a mini cupcake, and it's just happy cake sizes."

"I've purchased [it] a couple of times and gotta say it's worth the hype," wrote another.

"Omg it is soooooo good," another person commented. "I just came from a birthday party and had a slice. I thought I had died and gone to heaven."

"Yes, it's GOATed," answered another Redditor.

Some people chimed in to say they routinely buy the cake for birthday parties, while another person said, "We order this cake for every function!" 

Other forums contain copycat recipes aimed at recreating the cake at home.

TikTok food reviewer @leiahwithdacamry described the cake as "healthy almost, but it's still sweet and good," she said. "If you have a Whole Foods near you, you need to get this."

The Whole Foods website offers a history of the beloved cake, which is sold at all its stores nationwide and is the company's top-selling cake.

"This cake first made its debut 13 years ago at the Arabella Station store in New Orleans, where one of our talented bakery team members formulated a recipe based on her grandmother's original creation," it says. "It was an instant hit, and other stores picked up the recipe."

Multiple outlets have reported employee Chaya Conrad developed the recipe in 2002. The cakes took off across the South before being introduced nationwide, according to the Food Network.

In 2024, outraged customers took to social media accusing Whole Foods of changing the cake's recipe. 

One X user wrote, "You are ruining my life."

The company acknowledged it had "recently aligned the flavor profile, size, packaging and price" of the cake.

Later, however, Whole Foods said in a statement that, "Based on feedback from our customers, we will reintroduce single slices of the Berry Chantilly Cake that are the same as the classic our customers know and love."

Whole Foods recently launched the Next Generation Farmer Fund to support farmers under age 40 with funding and technical assistance for sustainable farming practices.

item.title: Morgan Fairchild says two men once abducted her off NYC street as bystanders laughed
item.description: Morgan Fairchild reveals on her new podcast how she joked her way to freedom in 1970 after being abducted off a New York City street while visiting her sister.
item.content:encoded:
Morgan Fairchild believes her sense of humor may have saved her life.

The actress, whose role on "Flamingo Road" cemented her bombshell image before she became a glamorous vixen on "Falcon Crest," has a new podcast, "2 B----es From Texas," co-hosted with her sister, Cathryn Hartt. The show features never-before-heard stories from their decades in showbiz and sit-down interviews with celebrity friends.

On a recent episode, Fairchild recalled being abducted on a New York City street before fame came calling. While it was no laughing matter, Fairchild said she managed to joke her way to freedom.

MORGAN FAIRCHILD REFUSED TO ‘SELL MY SOUL’ FOR HOLLYWOOD FAME

The then-20-year-old Dallas native was visiting her sister in 1970 when the terrifying ordeal unfolded.

"I'm walking up at two o'clock in the afternoon, broad daylight, no reason to be scared," Fairchild recalled to Fox News Digital.

"And this one big guy comes up talking to me. Now, I'm from Texas, but I know you're not supposed to talk to people on the street in New York. You don't talk to gentlemen. So I'm just ignoring him. And then this other big guy comes up on the other side of me. And these guys are both over six feet tall. They just grabbed me up by the elbows and threw me in this cab that was loitering there that I hadn't noticed."

WATCH: LORENZO LAMAS SHARES HOW HE MANAGES THE PRESSURES OF FAME

Fairchild said several people were waiting at a nearby bus stop, while others were walking by. Realizing she was in danger, she screamed for help. Fairchild said they must have thought she was "a hooker or something."

"Nobody lifted a finger," she said. "In fact, some of them laughed. And that made me realize how easy it would be to totally disappear and nobody would ever know what happened to you."

"The cab has very thick plexiglass between the passengers and the driver," Fairchild recalled. "I don't think the driver spoke much English. But these guys started telling me all the things they were going to do to me. That's how I found out that one was a pimp and the other was a pusher. The one who was a pusher was telling me all the things he was going to shoot me up with. And the pimp was telling me all the things that he was going to do to my body."

"I was a shy kid, but I was damned if I was going to let them see how scared I was," Fairchild added.

Fairchild said that every time her abductors described what they were going to do to her, she responded with "a wisecrack."

"I had them laughing," Fairchild said. "At one point, unbelievably to me, one of them looked at the other and said, 'She's funny. Let's let her go.' And they did. They gave the cab driver some money and said, 'Take her wherever she wants to go.' Well, I went back to my sister's apartment."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I didn't come out for three days," she admitted. "Intro to New York 101. It was very, very scary."

Fairchild still wonders how she managed to think so quickly while fearing for her life.

"I have no clue," she said. "It was all intuitive because I was not going to let them see how scared I was. That's what I did. I had to talk my way out of it by being funny, just being a wise a--. It's like an improvisation class. Somebody says something, and you come up with something else and make the scene work. It's like that, only much more dangerous. I've talked my way out of things a couple of times in my life just by being a wise a--."

"My sister had been living in New York for a little bit," she said. "I was the naïve one from Texas. Although naïve doesn't really cover it because I wasn't doing anything stupid. I was just walking in broad daylight. It wasn't in a dark alley, coming out of a club drunk or any of those other things that could make you vulnerable."

Fairchild said she shared the story on her podcast to encourage women to be aware of their surroundings.

"I think what women really need to keep in mind is how easy it is for you to just disappear," said Fairchild. "People were laughing at me as they were throwing me into this car. That, to me, was one of the scariest things: the lack of feeling for your fellow man. And you don’t think something like this could really ever happen to you."

The experience has stayed with Fairchild. To this day, she keeps watch on her surroundings.

item.title: Colorado's socialist surge shakes up the Democratic establishment
item.description: A veteran Colorado political insider warned the Democratic Socialists' rise in Denver mirrors the MAGA movement and could become a cancer for Democrats.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros shocked Colorado’s Democratic establishment when she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the state's June primary. The double-digit win exposed a growing rift over the party's values that has left some Democrats stunned and questioning the future of the party.

"If you had told me this woman would have won by 13 points, I would have bet my house against that," Doug Friednash, a veteran political strategist in Colorado, told Fox News Digital. "I never would have thought we would have seen a victory of that magnitude here in Denver."

Friednash has tracked Colorado's political shift from red to deep blue over the past three decades, previously serving in the state legislature representing House District 10 in Denver. He later served as Denver city attorney and chief of staff to former Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, and he currently works as a partner at Brownstein, a prominent legal and lobbying firm in the region.

Kiros' victory was one of dozens of wins for far-left candidates in Democratic primary elections this cycle as socialists continue to ascend across the country. The far-left's rise in the party has alarmed seasoned Democrats like Friednash.

JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS

"It was one thing watching this happen in New York ... But when it happens in a state like Colorado, which is really the gateway to the West, it tells me that this issue is going to spread and may be a cancer to the Democratic Party if they don't figure out what our values are," Friednash said.

He noted that Kiros' victory did not happen in a vacuum, pointing out that DSA-backed candidates have successfully captured seats in the state legislature and city councils over the past few years.

While Friednash originally predicted Rep. Diana DeGette would win, he acknowledged Kiros' campaign had a strong ground game and was able to tap into anti-establishment sentiments among progressives in the region. Kiros' team reportedly knocked on more than 100,000 voters' doors and ran a phone bank reaching 500,000 people leading up to election night.

SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM

She also campaigned on fighting for universal healthcare, affordable housing, utilities and more.

Friednash said Kiros' message resonated with younger voters who are frustrated by the high cost of living and feel let down by the Democratic establishment.

"I think the number one issue is affordability, by far," he said. "A lot of younger people that have moved to Denver have come here wanting to buy a house. They can't buy a home, it seems unaffordable and unattainable. And I think she's tapped into a lot of voter anger and hostility over things not being better."

He believes Denver has become a microcosm of the national debate taking place within the Democratic Party over its future direction. Comparing the DSA wave to the rise of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, Friednash warned that if party leadership refuses to call out the group's extreme policies, it will ultimately hurt Democrats in swing districts across the nation.

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN'

"As I look out at what's happening within the Democratic Party, you know, it's kind of like a ship without a captain," Friednash said. "A lot of the more mainstream Democrats, rather than trying to say, 'Here are the issues we should be fighting about,' are embracing the socialists, because I think they're afraid of them... much like I think we've seen with the MAGA movement."

"While some Democrats may be falling in love with socialism, you know who isn't? The rest of America," he continued. "That dog's not gonna hunt in these more competitive primaries."

Prominent centrist Democratic groups such as Third Way share that anxiety. The organization recently told The New York Times it plans to launch a $15 million campaign to combat the Democratic Socialists of America movement, which it believes poses a "mortal danger" to Democrats and will hurt the party in potential presidential swing states.

Concerns over the party's ideological turn aren't limited to establishment Democrats.

Jon Caldara, president of the Denver-based free-market think tank Independence Institute, also questions the future of his home state as democratic socialists continue to rise in prominence.

"Without a doubt, the Democratic Party in Colorado has changed," Caldara told Fox News Digital, arguing the state has abandoned its historically pro-business stance.

Caldara, a libertarian and longtime radio host and columnist, is outspoken about the challenges facing Denver and the broader state, such as affordability, homelessness and an exodus of businesses. He believes these issues will worsen, warning that establishment Democrats have lost control of their own party.

"When the state started turning left, this machine was so powerful, it really couldn't stop itself," Caldara said. "And now it's really beginning to eat their own. It's kind of a French Revolution thing that you see that the Democratic Party here in Colorado is now well out over their skis. And there is a growing fight between Democrats and socialists."

"The real telltale is that Democrats are afraid to speak the truth because they don't want to get canceled," he added. "It is vicious to go against the socialists."

SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'

Caldara believes younger voters are increasingly being drawn to democratic socialist candidates in Denver and across the country because they lack historical context for how these types of policies have fared across the world.

"Sadly, the young suffer from a terrible disease: It's called youth. And because they're young, they haven't seen failed socialism around the globe," Caldara said. "They haven't seen what happened in the Soviet Union. They haven't learned the lesson of Sweden, which looked like such a wonderful socialist paradise until it didn't work, and now they're turning into a capitalist system. They haven't seen this."

"So the idea that we can just redistribute rich guys' money sounds great," he continued. "We'll just do rent control. We'll do government funding. We all know how that's going to end up. It's going to end up poorly. And young people are going to be hurt."

"I'm sad that they want to run this experiment again," he added. "And it's even sadder that it's happening in this beautiful free state, this western state, this pro-free-enterprise state of Colorado."

Longtime Colorado residents like Gene Maine understand full well why socialist policies are appealing. But having fled the Soviet Union as a teenager in 1981, Maine sees unsettling parallels between the society he grew up in and the direction Denver is headed.

As a child, Maine said he was often told that America, Western Europe and capitalism were evil. But as he got older, he realized the utopian society he was supposedly living in wasn't all that it was cracked up to be.

REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP'

"As I grew older, I started recognizing that, ‘Oh my God, I'm being lied to. We're all being lied to," Maine recalled. "This is not the freest society in the world. It's a jail."

After defecting from the USSR with his mother as a teenager, Maine lived in Los Angeles before settling in Erie, Colorado in the 1990s, where he’s lived since, raising his family and working as an engineer.

Over the past three decades, Maine has watched Denver change from a small "cow town" into a large municipality, and witnessed a corresponding political shift as the population boomed.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

"All of a sudden, it wasn't, 'Can we have the smallest government possible and leave us alone?' It became, 'Well, we need to give you free stuff.' And that's when I started to worry a little bit," Maine said.

Maine isn't surprised that veteran Democrats are facing primary threats from the far left, noting that Kiros’ campaign benefited from a well-organized ground game and sweeping promises on healthcare and affordability that drew in younger voters.

"She is winning the primary because we have an organized group convincing people that they can have free stuff. You can have free medical care. You can have free supermarkets. You can have free transportation. And it's very appealing," Maine explained. "I like free stuff, but what they forget to tell you is that nothing is really free. As they say, there's no free lunch."

SOCIALIST HOUSE CANDIDATE SAYS HE AGREES WITH REPUBLICANS ON 'ONE ISSUE'

He believes historical lessons are being lost as generations grow further removed from the realities of the Soviet Union.

"So there is a gap that's being exploited," he continued. "And it's been exploited from internal and from external, because there's a lot of evil forces in the world that do not want America to succeed."

While critics view the rise of the DSA as a dangerous departure from American values, Kiros and other DSA candidates argue their policies are a pragmatic response to liberal voters fed up with how the Democratic Party has responded to their struggles.

Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS’s "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover that there is room in the party for various viewpoints.

"Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right?"

"Until a self-proclaimed communist actually wins an election, then it’s just noise from the Republican Party. There’s no one who’s actually winning with that," she continued.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Kiros denied being a communist herself, arguing that younger voters are embracing the DSA message because, at its core, it represents "economic populism."

Her campaign centered on Medicare for all, universal childcare, investments in public housing, higher federal taxes on the wealthy, publicly owned utilities and more. Like many other socialist campaigns across the country, she is also firmly anti-Israel. 

Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats, and the Working Families Party.

Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77 percent of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado.

Kiros’s campaign and the DSA did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: Trump pumps brakes on Senate budget plan, delaying GOP SAVE America push
item.description: Senate Republicans left D.C. without passing the SAVE America Act as Trump intervened on the budget reconciliation vote over concerns it would fail.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Republicans may have left Washington on a high note early Saturday morning, but they left one major item on the table: passing the SAVE America Act.

It’s the bill that has dominated President Donald Trump’s attention span and garnered heavy criticism against Republicans in the upper chamber for not being able to pass it.

And despite guarantees from some in the party that they would object to leaving until Sept. in order to pass the voter integrity bill, lawmakers’ suitcases were packed and ready for the airport. It’s one of several agenda items that didn’t get finished prior to the lawmakers' vacation, and one that will have to wait until next month. But its biggest proponents appear okay with that outcome.

SCHUMER CAVES, HANDS REPUBLICANS SHUTDOWN WIN AFTER MONTHS OF UNCERTAINTY

"We’re not dropping SAVE," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, said. "It’s a matter of time."

Time between now and the end of this session of Congress will be an increasingly short commodity to come by.

The Senate returns the third week of September and will be tasked with moving two massive bills dealing with cryptocurrency regulations and money in college sports, both of which didn't make the cut during the upper chamber’s last week in town.

Then they’ll leave once again for nearly the entire month of October in preparation for midterm elections in early November.

SCHUMER SAID ‘DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID’ — THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL

Another priority heavily pushed by Trump and the administration, taking another crack at the party line budget reconciliation process, was detoured, too.

That process is how Republicans hope to pass the SAVE America Act without Democrats getting the chance to block it with the filibuster. Republicans were ready to vote on the $150 billion budget blueprint drafted by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., until Trump intervened over concerns that it would fail.

The push was paused after Johnson, who just took over the Senate Budget Committee, Lee and Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., huddled in the office of Senate Majority Leader John Thune after speaking with Trump.

Johnson said Trump agreed that the best path forward was to "just work diligently through August into September to do an actually better budget reconciliation bill."

Republicans want to crank up the defense spending in their budget framework — Johnson said that War Secretary Pete Hegseth made a "very convincing case" to beef up the funding by $350 billion as the war in Iran continues and munitions dwindle.

Still, whether the gamble to incentivize states to take up portions of the SAVE America Act will work remains unknown, given that the Senate’s rules chief will ultimately decide if the provisions pass muster with reconciliation’s guardrails.

BLANCHE SURVIVES REPUBLICAN DEFECTORS AS TRUMP GETS HIS NEW ATTORNEY GENERAL

Taking another shot at reconciliation that doesn’t include cost-of-living elements or affordability-minded provisions hasn’t been a popular subject among Senate Republicans, especially heading into midterms.

Thune acknowledged that there was an appetite among Republicans to use the legislative tool to muscle through defense funding and try to include elements of the SAVE America Act.

The top Senate Republican, unlike others in his conference, hasn’t been gung-ho about turning to reconciliation for a third time. That appeared to subtly change early Saturday morning.

"I think at some point, we’re going to need to do another reconciliation bill," Thune said.

Meanwhile, Republicans were able to accomplish several items on their to-do list Saturday morning.

They passed a short-term funding extension until early December to take away Democrats’ ability to politicize another government shutdown, advanced a bone-crushing Russia sanctions package and confirmed acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to lead the Department of Justice with the command of a Senate-confirmed cabinet member.

But Democrats blocked a voter ID bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, and hurdles remained for the massive, cryptocurrency bill known as the Clarity Act, and Sen. Ted Cruz’s, R-Texas, legislation going after Name Image and Likeness (NIL) funding in college sports.

Perhaps the most glaring omission, however, was a vote on whether to cancel the August recess.

Lee had pushed for a full vote on the Senate floor as part of the Senate’s push to reach a broader agreement on several legislative items. Instead, he accepted a voice vote, uttering a quiet "no," on the floor against the forthcoming recess.

"Would it have been better if we had passed SAVE America already? Absolutely," Lee said. "Would it be better if we had the votes right now? Yes. We, for a variety of reasons, don't have the wherewithal to pass it right now."

"No, no, no, [its] Democrats," Johnson interjected. "The reason is Democrats. Democrats refuse to vote for any kind of voter integrity measure, that’s just the reality of the situation."

item.title: I got stage 4 cancer in my 40s. My young daughter and husband keep me fighting

item.content:encoded:
When I was first diagnosed with rare metastatic appendiceal cancer in October 2023, my world blew up. It was a diagnosis with no known cure and no specific treatment protocol. Talk about shattered dreams. I had just turned 40 and had been married only three years. My daughter wasn’t even 2 years old yet. Later, I wrote about my fierce determination to fight for my husband and young daughter because I had "too much to lose." At the time, my entire existence shrunk to a single, desperate objective: Do everything possible to beat cancer.

So, I suited up for battle. Over the past nearly three years, I’ve lost count of the rounds of chemotherapy I’ve endured. Maybe 45? Alongside the chemo came multiple surgeries, constant scans, port placements, hernias, drains, stents, bags, a 30-pound weight loss, and lots of flights back and forth to Texas for a targeted treatment. My life is lived day to day.

And yet, the world doesn't stop turning just because you have stage 4 cancer.

I'M A 40-YEAR-OLD MOM AND WIFE WITH STAGE 4 CANCER. HERE'S WHAT I WANT YOU TO KNOW

All of this medical warfare happens while I am still mothering a spunky 4-year-old girl who is my entire world. It happens while I am trying to be a present wife, take care of a house, work as a journalist, be a supportive daughter to ailing parents, and desperately claw at whatever energy I have left to do the things I love.

The whiplash of these transitions is where the real exhaustion lives. In the span of a single week, I can fly to Texas, sit in a cold, sterile infusion room, fly back to New Jersey, spend two days with my head in a toilet bowl, and then force myself up to play dress-up with my daughter, take her to dance class, buy groceries, and run the everyday errands a healthy person takes for granted. Then, if I'm lucky, my husband, daughter, and I get a brief window to do "normal" family things before the entire brutal cycle resets.

When there is no end in sight—no definitive light at the end of the tunnel—the weight of that routine feels crushing. Factor in sudden setbacks such as unexpected hospital stays, and any remaining sense of control simply vanishes. Chasing down clinical trials feels like another full-time job.

I'M 41 WITH A HUSBAND AND CHILD. I HAVE TOO MUCH TO LOSE AND WON'T GIVE UP MY FIGHT AGAINST CANCER

This isn't about "staying positive" or "being strong." This is the grueling reality of cancer. You either choose to face it, or you quit and wither away. I refuse to quit, no matter how many roadblocks are thrown in my path. But refusing to quit doesn’t mean I don’t break. I allow myself to cry, and I allow myself to get angry. 

Unfortunately, the people closest to me have to witness that raw ugliness. They see the messy tears; they bear the brunt of the moments I snap and scream. It is what it is. Luckily, the people who regularly witness my breakdowns understand the toll of this siege, and they keep showing up for me and my family anyway. I am profoundly grateful that they do.

People often ask why I don’t just take a leave of absence and step away from work, or how I manage to keep parenting through the physical wreckage of ongoing treatment. The answer is simple: These roles are the anchors keeping me tethered to who I am.

I love my job. I often work during my infusions because it is therapeutic; it forces my mind off oncology timelines. And when it comes to parenting, my husband and I are blessed with a smart, empathetic, healthy little girl. But as she gets older, the boundaries of her innocence are tested. We find ourselves having to explain more. We talk about the scars and bumps on my "Frankenstein tummy." We talk about God and angels.

PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS

Behind closed doors, my husband and I have to navigate the terrifying conversations you hope you will never have in a lifetime. Sometimes, the heaviest things go entirely unsaid because we are both paralyzed by the exact same fears. That, too, is the reality of fighting cancer with a young child in the house.

Back in 2023, after my first few infusions, I envisioned victory as a traditional finish line: a clean scan, a final treatment, a definitive surgery that removes every cancer cell. Today, I have to accept the reality that those specific victories are unlikely.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

But I have learned that a lack of a cure does not mean a lack of victory. My definition of a "win" has simply evolved.

Now, a win looks like having enough strength to be out on the ice, at the beach or on the ski slopes with my family. It looks like making it through the afternoon without needing a nap before picking up my daughter from school. It’s finishing a workout or staying up late with my husband watching "The Sopranos" reruns. It’s completing normal, everyday tasks.

When I was first diagnosed, a friend who was intimately familiar with cancer told me, "This is just a chapter in your life story." It has turned out to be an incredibly long, gritty, painful chapter. But the truth is, none of us truly know when our story will end. 

I am still fighting, still working, and still loving with everything I have—and I am praying for many more chapters to come.

item.title: From Iron Dome to Abraham Accords: Congressional trips helped shape 15 years of US-Israel cooperation
item.description: USIEA has brought dozens of lawmakers to Israel over 15 years, shaping major congressional action on Iron Dome funding and military cooperation.
item.content:encoded:
For 15 years, dozens of American lawmakers have had the opportunity to see one of the country's most important — and increasingly debated — alliances firsthand. Since 2011, the U.S.-Israel Education Association (USIEA) has brought members of Congress to Israel, giving them an on-the-ground look at the security, technology and geopolitical issues that often come before them in Washington.

USIEA Founder and President Heather Johnston reflected on the organization's 15th anniversary in a conversation with Fox News Digital. She recalled meeting then-Majority Leader Eric Cantor and presenting him with a list of objectives to advance educational trips to Israel for U.S. lawmakers.

"He was flabbergasted because he had been looking for somebody for two years that could lead those tours," Johnston said.

OPINION: THE US-ISRAEL STRATEGIC ALLIANCE – PARTNERSHIP, NOT CHARITY

The organization's first tour included five members of the House Armed Services Committee, and they were shown a brand-new piece of missile defense technology that Johnston said was "just barely off the ground" at the time. The system, known as the Iron Dome, was so new at the time that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had to declassify it, so American lawmakers could see the state-of-the-art tech.

Johnston said that the lawmakers were so impressed with Iron Dome's capabilities that they began the groundwork to increase funding for it. Within a matter of weeks after returning to Washington, the five members of the House Armed Services Committee met with 54 members of Congress. The result came less than three months later when the lawmakers succeeded in tripling the budget for Iron Dome.

"Our commitment to the security of Israel is rock solid. And as I've said to the Prime Minister in every single one of our meetings, the United States will always have Israel's back when it comes to Israel's security," Obama said at the time.

HUCKABEE WARNS OF 'BIBLICAL IGNORANCE' AS HE DEFENDS CONSERVATIVE SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL

BRUCE PEARL EXPLAINS WHY HE REFUSES TO STAY SILENT ON ISRAEL AND ANTISEMITISM

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Netanyahu credited Johnston and USIEA with helping strengthen the U.S.-Israel alliance.

"For 15 years, Heather Johnston and USIEA have stood proudly for Israel and for the right of the Jewish people to live in our ancestral homeland," Netanyahu said. "USIEA helped secure support for important American-Israeli joint projects, which contributed to the benefit of the great American-Israeli alliance."

The Iron Dome funding increase would become one of the many milestones Johnston points to when firsthand exposure preceded major congressional action on U.S.-Israel cooperation. Over the course of 15 years, USIEA expanded its trips as the alliance evolved through multiple administrations, the Abraham Accords and the Hamas-led Oct. 7 massacre.

Former U.S. Ambassador to Israel David Friedman described the relationship between Washington and Jerusalem over the last 15 years as an "EKG," saying that it involved "lots of ups and downs."

"I think if you sort of drew a trend line, it's gotten very strong," he told Fox News Digital.

HOLY LAND BATTLE: SOLOMON'S POOLS BECOME FLASHPOINT IN FIGHT OVER ISRAEL'S BIBLICAL HERITAGE

Friedman said he interacted with USIEA after his nomination as he worked to educate himself on the ties between the U.S. and Israel. During his interactions with the organization, he was struck by USIEA's focus on practicality.

"They were deeply schooled and understood what needed to get done," he said, citing efforts ranging from Iron Dome funding to establishing an FDA office in Israel.

Friedman argued that over time American lawmakers increasingly saw Israel as a country that delivered "real value to the United States in terms of technology, medicine, national security." He believes both sides of the aisle, outside of hot-button issues, have seen that the U.S. and Israel had much to gain from each other.

Current U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee echoed that assessment, arguing that many Americans underestimate the full extent of the U.S.-Israel relationship.

"I don't think most Americans really fully comprehend the depth of the partnership that the U.S. and Israel has," he told Fox Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Huckabee noted that this partnership played out in a variety of areas, including military cooperation, especially as both worked to stop the Iranian regime from gaining nuclear arms.

"During the two different operations against Iran both last summer — 2025 — and then this year, the six and a half weeks starting in late February, our planes were flying wingtip to wingtips and our military operations were basically a room full of people both Israeli and American whose joint operations were truly something to behold," he said.

But Huckabee said the value of organizations like USIEA extends beyond showcasing military cooperation. He argued that bringing lawmakers to Israel allows them to see realities on the ground that can be difficult to grasp from Washington alone.

"A lot of the lies about Israel are completely debunked pretty quickly," Huckabee said.

As one example, Huckabee pointed to Israel's Arab citizens serving in senior positions throughout society, including in the Knesset, on the Supreme Court and in the Israel Defense Forces, saying those experiences often challenge preconceptions held by visitors.

Looking ahead, Johnston said she believes the organization's mission is becoming more important as the U.S.-Israel relationship expands beyond the traditional sense of cooperation.

"A lot of what we do is very pioneering. We're not just bringing on education that already exists and showing them what already exists in the collaboration, but really showing them what is to come," she said.

item.title: Democratic socialist Francesca Hong has former child star, OnlyFans model in senior campaign role: report
item.description: An OnlyFans model and sex worker advocate is reportedly serving as deputy campaign manager for Francesca Hong's Wisconsin governor campaign.
item.content:encoded:
Former child actress and OnlyFans model Renee Olstead is reportedly serving in a senior role on Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong's gubernatorial campaign ahead of next week's Democratic primary.

Olstead, who also goes by Renee Faust, is serving as Hong's deputy campaign manager, according to The Heartland Post. Hong, a Democratic socialist, is among the candidates competing in next week's Democratic gubernatorial primary.

The outlet reported that Olstead has worked as a paid campaign operative since at least January. Her X bio reads "HONG 4 GOV" and links to Hong's get-out-the-vote page.

Her social media account also features photos from campaign events, and The Heartland Post reported that she has coordinated logistics for high-profile surrogates, including streamer and political commentator Hasan Piker.

FRANCESCA HONG REMARKS THANKSGIVING IS HER 'FAVORITE HOLIDAY,' ANSWERS SHE DOES NOT 'WANT TO CANCEL IT'

Fox News Digital asked Hong's campaign to confirm Olstead's title and responsibilities, when she began working for the campaign, whether she is a paid employee and her qualifications for the role. The campaign responded with a statement but did not directly address each question.

"Renee Faust is a licensed mental health clinician who has spent her career providing care to trafficking survivors," the campaign said. "Since joining the campaign in December, she has helped build the largest grassroots campaign in Wisconsin history. The right-wing politicians attacking her are the same ones who want government dictating women's health care decisions."

Olstead previously founded the Coalition for American Sex Workers (CASW – LOCAL 304), which advocates for decriminalization and other policy changes affecting sex workers.

Last year, Hong and three other state representatives presented Olstead with an official Wisconsin State Assembly citation recognizing her advocacy for sex workers' rights and her selection as "Penthouse Pet of the Year" in 2024.

CONTROVERSIAL SOCIALIST CHEF FLIP-FLOPS ON ABOLISH THE POLICE, SAYS SHE’S ‘SERIOUS ABOUT PUBLIC SAFETY’

The campaign did not directly respond to a separate question from Fox News Digital asking Hong to explain her decision to participate in presenting Olstead with the citation and what she intended to recognize.

Hong has also pursued legislation that would decriminalize prostitution involving adults and establish a sex workers' bill of rights.

Wisconsin Family Action, a conservative advocacy organization based in Madison, criticized Olstead's involvement in Hong's campaign.

"Wisconsinites deserve to have serious people leading the state. It is unbelievable to see that the likely Democratic nominee for governor has an active sex worker leading her campaign," Daniel Degner, president of Wisconsin Family Action, said in a statement. "Voters deserve to know whether if Hong is elected, she will elevate a porn star to leadership in her administration."

SANDERS' ANSWER WHEN ASKED IF HE WILL ENDORSE SOCIALIST HONG IN WISCONSIN SPARKS INSTANT MOCKERY: 'SAYS A LOT'

Hong has previously expressed support on social media for progressive proposals including abolishing the U.S. Senate and defunding the police, though she has recently distanced herself from some of those positions in interviews ahead of Tuesday's gubernatorial primary.

Hong faces Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, former Wisconsin Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan and Democratic state Sen. Kelda Roys in the primary.

Hong also faced renewed scrutiny over a since-deleted 2020 X post calling to "cancel Thanksgiving" in order to "stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed Indegenous [sic] folx and women."

She recently distanced herself from the post, telling Politico that Thanksgiving is her "favorite holiday" and that she does not want to cancel it.

"My favorite holiday is Thanksgiving," Hong told Politico Playbook. "Yep, I don't want to cancel it. I actually love it."

Fox News Digital's Andrew Mark Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Schumer said ‘Democrats support voter ID’ — then every Senate Democrat voted against GOP bill
item.description: Chuck Schumer and Senate Democrats blocked Jon Husted's voter ID bill despite Schumer's past claims that Democrats support voter identification.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats blocked a key component of the SAVE America Act that, in the past, they have supported.

During the wee hours of Saturday morning, Senate Republicans tried and failed to get Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his colleagues to back a stripped back voter ID bill amid a spree of last-minute legislative business.

But Senate Democrats, including Schumer, have for years espoused support for identification to vote. Several states with Democratic senators have voter ID laws, too.

SCHUMER, DEMOCRATS SAY THEY SUPPORT VOTER ID, THEN BLOCK GOP AMENDMENT TO REQUIRE IT

"Democrats support voter ID," Schumer said in March. "In fact, we included it, and it is included, in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago."

Schumer and his entire caucus voted against the bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, nonetheless. Requiring identification is already the practice in 36 states. Of those, 23 require photo ID, while 13 accept another form of identification, such as a bank statement. Nine of those states have Democratic senators.

It was the last stand of the night for the Senate, which is gearing up to leave Washington, D.C., for several weeks of valuable campaign time in vulnerable incumbents’ home states.

SENATE REPUBLICANS PUSH ELECTION DAY DEADLINE FOR CALIFORNIA'S MARATHON BALLOT COUNTS

And it comes as Republicans have so far tried and failed to find a path forward for the SAVE America Act, which Democrats, along with a handful from the GOP, have blocked numerous times in a variety of configurations.

Husted’s bill would have prohibited state and local election officials from providing a ballot to vote in federal elections unless a person provided a valid form of identification.

Husted’s bill teed up a plethora of options, including an unexpired driver’s license with a photo, an unexpired state-issued ID card with a photo, a valid passport, a valid military or veteran ID with a photo or an unexpired tribal ID with a photo.

It’s also not the first time Democrats have blocked it. In March, Republicans tested their support of voter ID for the first time in a vote to attach Husted’s bill to the SAVE America Act. It failed on party lines then, too.

TRUMP KEEPS CALLING THUNE DESPITE PUBLIC FIGHT OVER SAVE AMERICA ACT

After it became clear that President Donald Trump’s top legislative priority was not going to be passed nor even considered before lawmakers exit Washington, D.C., Republicans opted to take one last crack at Democrats' resolve.

"We've got many Democrats, who have said, ‘I’m just fine with voter ID,’" Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, said. "Voter ID is a major component of SAVE America, and they've said that over and over again when we had it on the floor in late February and early March."

"It was the argument that I heard from many of these people, as it was on the floor for hours and hours at a time, saying, ‘I'm okay with voter ID, don't like this,’" he continued. "So we're gonna find out where they are."

Lee has been the loudest supporter of the SAVE America Act in the Senate, pushing and prodding his colleagues on X to get on board with passing the package.

Republicans had a chance earlier in the night to begin the work of crafting a version of the SAVE America Act with a budget blueprint that, if successful, would have teed up the partyline budget reconciliation process, but were called to stand down by Trump.

Now, they don’t return until early September, just weeks out from a midterm election that could reshape the balance of power in the Senate.

item.title: Former Miss North Carolina USA says conservative Christian values played role in losing crown
item.description: Brittany Boltinhouse says she believes her conservative Christian values led to being stripped of her Miss North Carolina USA pageant crown.
item.content:encoded:
Former Miss North Carolina USA Brittany Boltinhouse is speaking out after being stripped of her crown weeks before the Miss USA pageant, saying she believes her conservative Christian values played a role in the decision.

The Miss USA Organization announced Aug. 5 that Boltinhouse had been stripped of her title. Chairman Thom Brodeur did not specify the conduct behind the decision but said the organization "does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia nor language that strips any person of their dignity," adding that the conduct occurred "over an extended period of time."

The decision ended Boltinhouse's reign just weeks after she won the state title and less than three weeks before she was scheduled to represent North Carolina at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant on Aug. 27.

In an interview Friday with the Carolina Journal, Boltinhouse called losing the title a "blessing in disguise."

MISS NORTH CAROLINA USA LOSES CROWN AFTER ORGANIZER CONDEMNS 'RACISM, HOMOPHOBIA, TRANSPHOBIA'

"I'm very much at peace and I'm actually glad it happened to me and not some other young lady that, you know, maybe just probably wouldn't make it through what I'm going through right now," Boltinhouse said. "The scrutiny, my family behind it as well. But I will say that I'm very much at peace and I see the light at the end of the tunnel and I know who I am and I know what I can become."

Boltinhouse said a confidentiality agreement prevents her from discussing the circumstances that led to her losing the title, but she said she believes her political and religious views played a role.

"I believe and think I was stripped from my title because of my political stance and my belief system as a conservative Christian woman," she said.

"I'm proud of my faith. I'm proud of my standards. I'm a proud conservative woman, but a Christian woman. I'm a God-fearing woman," Boltinhouse added.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES

Asked whether she believed being conservative was disqualifying in the pageant system, Boltinhouse said people should be free to express their political beliefs.

"I believe that everyone has a right to say what they want to say and feel the way they want to feel," she said.

Boltinhouse said she did not know whether her support for President Donald Trump played a role in the decision.

"I don't know. I don't know. All I can say from the information that I have today and what I believe and I think is honestly I don't know," Boltinhouse said. "I wasn't really given anything."

CHILLING NEW VIDEO SHOWS ARMED CITIZENS, OFF-DUTY TROOPER CONFRONT IN-N-OUT GUNMAN DURING DEADLY RAMPAGE

Despite losing her crown, Boltinhouse said she forgives the organization and hopes other women will view her experience as encouragement to stand by their beliefs.

"Hopefully see me as an example," she said. "To always stand for what you believe, no matter what, no matter where, no matter what you do."

"I speak to the women that even are not conservative, that they have the right to speak the way that you feel, no matter what platform, no matter what belief system that you may have," she added.

Myla Hadley, the first runner-up in the state competition, will represent North Carolina on the national stage "with our full confidence and our support," Brodeur said in a previous statement.

MORE THAN 50 BODIES FOUND DECOMPOSING INSIDE CHICAGO FUNERAL HOME AFTER NEIGHBORS COMPLAINED OF 'STENCH'

Brodeur said the decision was made in consultation with Boltinhouse, her state directors and the Miss USA Organization. He also emphasized that the organization did not view accountability as justification for personally attacking Boltinhouse.

"There is a young woman at the center of this," Brodeur said. "She has been named, examined, and judged in public in a way that most of us would not survive, and she is still a human being with a family, a future, and a life ahead of her that is longer than this part of her journey."

"I have never believed that accountability requires cruelty, or that holding a line means enjoying the fall of the person who crossed it," he continued.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Miss USA Organization for additional comment.

Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

item.title: MIKE DAVIS: Chuck Grassley's behind-the-scenes work proved decisive in Todd Blanche confirmation fight
item.description: Chuck Grassley's behind-the-scenes role proved decisive in securing Todd Blanche's confirmation as attorney general despite full Democrat opposition.
item.content:encoded:
By voting to confirm Todd Blanche as the 88th Attorney General of the United States, Senate Republicans delivered a major victory for President Donald Trump, the American people and the rule of law. Blanche will fulfill President Trump’s mandate to Make America Safe Again. The key cabinet confirmation provides much-needed unity and momentum for Trump and Senate Republicans — and a good opportunity for Trump to hard-reset his relationship with the Senate, so they can go on offense this fall.

Blanche’s proven track record as the deputy and acting attorney general leaves no doubt that Trump nominated the right man, at the right time, for the right job. But with full Democrat opposition, Blanche’s confirmation process was tougher than it should have been given his unmatched experience and sterling qualifications. Blanche is a longtime former federal prosecutor in the most prestigious U.S. attorney’s office and Big Law partner in New York City who put everything on the line to defend Trump against Biden’s unprecedented, republic-ending lawfare. Blanche helped Trump beat this. Trump now sits in the White House instead of a federal prison cell, running our country instead of appealing his bogus convictions.

For the last 17 months, Blanche has brought reforms and accountability to the Justice Department — so the Democrats’ politicized and weaponized injustice never happens again. These reforms and accountability must and will continue. Blanche will continue to take the Justice Department back to its most crucial basics: arresting, prosecuting and imprisoning violent criminals, government fraudsters and other real criminals — instead of hunting down parents, Christians and other political opponents like we witnessed under the Obama and Biden Justice Departments.

TRUMP'S AG PICK OFF LIFE SUPPORT AFTER KEY REPUBLICAN REBELS RELENT

Getting here wasn’t easy. There were bumps in the road and moments when the confirmation looked like it could stall. The reason it didn’t, and the reason Blanche is now America’s confirmed attorney general, is Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee.

When the nomination hit headwinds from Senators John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., both of whom raised good-faith concerns, it was Grassley who stepped in. He meditated. He bridged the gap. He kept all parties at the table. And he got the deal done.

Likewise, when Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., had principled objections to DOJ policy, he worked with Grassley, other Senate colleagues and the Trump administration to find a workable resolution. Susie Wiles, Trump’s highly respected White House chief of staff, is always the invaluable glue.

Blanche closed the deal with his personal diplomacy, as he demonstrated to Cassidy he is uniquely qualified. Cassidy deserves great credit for his willingness to put his country over personal differences. That’s what the Senate process looks like when it works. And it worked here because the right people were in the right roles.

No one did more to get Blanche confirmed than Grassley. Grassley works; Grassley delivers — especially for Trump. Whether it is nominations, taxes, trade or almost all the rest of Trump’s greatest Senate accomplishments, Grassley is the key. He never brags about it. Grassley just quietly works hard and gets the job done.

This is Grassley’s fourth Republican attorney general he’s confirmed as chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee. He brought more than four decades of institutional knowledge and experience from working on more than fifteen attorney general nominations since joining the committee. Grassley knows how to move a nomination through a committee full of competing agendas and a swamp press corps hungry for a Republican scalp.

In a town full of politicians looking to take credit for others’ work, Grassley stands out. He’s a work horse, not a show horse. Grassley exemplifies Iowa humility, so someone else has to brag for him. Blanche is now attorney general thanks to Grassley. And now Blanche can get back to work, fully Senate confirmed, continuing to help Trump Make America Safe Again.

The numbers don’t lie. The U.S. is approaching the lowest murder rate recorded since at least 1900. That’s according to the FBI’s own data, backed by the Council on Criminal Justice’s finding of a 21% drop in homicides from 2024 to 2025, with another 18% drop in the first half of 2026. We are living through a historic collapse in violent crime on President Trump’s watch.

Migrant encounters at the southern border hit their lowest level in more than 50 years, down from over two million under Biden to numbers not seen since 1970, according to Pew Research. We have control of our borders. Drug smuggling networks are being dismantled. Human traffickers are being prosecuted. Dangerous criminals — the ones Obama and Biden were too busy targeting conservatives to actually pursue — are being put away.

TODD BLANCHE EARNS ATTORNEY GENERAL BID ENDORSEMENT FROM LAW ENFORCEMENT ALLIANCE AHEAD OF CONFIRMATION

Biden and Obama treated the Department of Justice as a political weapon. And they pointed it at Trump. They pointed it at his allies. They pointed it at parents at school board meetings. They pointed it at Christians. Real criminals walked free while Democrats weaponized federal law enforcement against their political enemies for non-crimes. That ends with Todd Blanche.

Blanche is bringing real accountability — not the partisan, weaponized kind Obama and Biden practiced. He is reversing the politicization of the DOJ, not continuing it. His priorities are clear: prosecute illegal aliens, human traffickers, drug traffickers and dangerous criminals. Protect the American people. Hold bad actors accountable, including the ones in government. Never use the DOJ as a partisan sword. Ever. Again.

Trump made a bold choice in nominating Blanche. Not because Blanche isn’t qualified — he’s more qualified than anyone else for this role. But because the left was going to come at him hard, re-litigating every case and every decision. They tried. It didn’t work.

Trump’s instinct was right, as usual. He saw in Blanche what those of us in this fight have always seen: a man of genuine courage, deep experience and unshakeable commitment to the rule of law.

Blanche is the right man, for the right job, at the right moment in American history. He is a bold and fearless warrior for the Constitution who gave up millions in future earnings to stand in a courtroom and defend President Trump against the most weaponized, politically-motivated legal assault in American history. He bled for this fight and he won. That is the kind of person you want running the Department of Justice. And now the Senate has confirmed him.

America deserves a DOJ that fights for Americans, not for the political class, not for Democrat donors, not for the deep-state bureaucrats who spent decades building a machine that answers to no one. Blanche is going to change that. He already has.

Thankfully, Trump and Grassley made sure he got the chance.
